headline: A Designer's Shader Primer for AI-Era Browser Games
lede: Danny Limanseta, a product designer who co-founded Singapore's RedMart grocery delivery service, has spent the past year building browser games using AI coding assistants. Competing in the 2026 Cursor Vibe Jam — which requires that at least 90% of code be written by AI — he paused to publish a practical taxonomy of Three.js shader types for fellow vibe coders who want their games to look better without becoming graphics programmers.
body:
Limanseta is a product designer and serial entrepreneur — co-founder of RedMart and Give.asia, a Southeast Asian charitable fundraising platform — whose entry in the jam is *Tiny Skies*, a cosy flying game built on **Three.js**, the dominant JavaScript library for GPU-accelerated 3D graphics in the browser. With over 112,000 GitHub stars and a history stretching back to 2010, Three.js wraps *WebGL* — the browser's direct line to the GPU — in an accessible API. The 2026 Cursor Vibe Jam was organized by indie developer Pieter Levels, carried a $40,000 prize pool, and stipulated that at least 90% of code be AI-generated. The scarce resource, by design, is creative direction rather than code literacy.

A *shader* is a small program that runs on the GPU rather than the CPU, executing in massive parallel batches across thousands of cores simultaneously. In the WebGL pipeline that Three.js uses, two types do the fundamental work: the *vertex shader* transforms the 3D coordinates of each mesh point into 2D screen positions, while the *fragment shader* determines the color of each pixel. Both are written in *GLSL* (OpenGL Shading Language), a C-like language compiled at runtime for the GPU. Three.js's most recent release, r184, adds *TSL* (Three.js Shading Language), a JavaScript node-graph API that compiles down to GLSL — or to *WGSL* for newer *WebGPU*-based rendering — removing the need to write C-style syntax directly. This is the infrastructure that makes Limanseta's suggestion viable: describe the effect to an AI, and the AI can produce the GLSL.

Two of the five shader types he recommends exploit mathematical tricks that are cheap to compute but visually convincing. **Perlin noise** — invented by Ken Perlin in the early 1980s while working on the film *Tron*, work that earned him an Academy Award — produces smooth, organic randomness without blocky artifacts. Fed as a time-varying function into a *fragment shader*, it distorts texture sampling coordinates to simulate the shimmer and refraction of a water surface. *Simplex noise*, Perlin's own 2001 improvement, uses triangular grid cells rather than square ones, generating fewer directional artifacts at lower computational cost. The *Fresnel shader* is grounded in actual optics: the reflectivity of most surfaces increases sharply at oblique viewing angles, so at the silhouette edges of a 3D object the shader brightens a narrow rim, producing the glowing halo that separates a character or spaceship from the background. The computation reduces to a dot product and an exponent — one of the most cost-effective visual improvements available in real-time 3D.

*Post-processing shaders* operate on the fully rendered 2D image rather than on geometry — analogous to color grading applied to film after shooting. Three.js manages these via *EffectComposer*, a pipeline that chains passes in sequence: a RenderPass captures the raw 3D output, then additional ShaderPasses stack effects before the frame reaches the screen. The VHS-style distortion that Limanseta credits to Pieter Levels's game *Drones of War* — an *FPV* drone combat simulator built during the jam — uses procedural noise to simulate horizontal line displacement, vertical roll, and analog grain, mimicking either a degraded cassette tape or, in the game's conceit, an FPV video link losing fidelity with distance. The canonical Three.js implementation is Felix Turner's *BadTV shader*, which runs as an EffectComposer pass. *Vertex displacement*, the fifth type Limanseta names, works at the geometry stage rather than the image stage: the vertex shader pushes mesh points away from their rest positions according to a noise or wave function, making trees sway or objects wobble without requiring additional geometry.

Limanseta's broader point is that this toolkit — once the province of specialist graphics engineers — is now accessible to anyone who can describe visual intent to an AI. The combination of Three.js's abstraction layer, TSL's node-graph API, and large language models that can generate GLSL on demand has flattened a steep learning curve. The jam's AI-mandatory rule is, in this reading, less a novelty constraint and more a proof of concept: the limiting factor in making a visually polished browser game is no longer the ability to write shader code.

concepts.definition: A small program that runs directly on the GPU, executing in parallel across thousands of cores simultaneously. In WebGL, vertex shaders transform 3D geometry into 2D screen positions; fragment shaders calculate the final color of each pixel.

One of the two fundamental shader types in the WebGL pipeline. Runs once per vertex — each corner point of a 3D mesh — transforming world coordinates into screen positions. Can also displace vertices to animate geometry, as in tree-sway or wave effects.

The second fundamental shader type in the WebGL pipeline. Runs once per pixel fragment of a rendered surface, computing the final output color by sampling textures, applying lighting equations, and combining material properties.

OpenGL Shading Language — a C-like language for writing GPU shader programs. In Three.js, vertex and fragment shaders are written in GLSL strings and compiled at runtime for the graphics card. The new TSL API abstracts this syntax away.

A browser API that exposes GPU-accelerated graphics to JavaScript, based on OpenGL ES. Three.js uses WebGL as its primary renderer, enabling hardware-accelerated 3D in the browser without plugins. Three.js r118 moved to WebGL 2.0 by default.

A JavaScript node-graph API stable in Three.js r184 that lets developers compose shader logic using function chaining instead of raw GLSL strings. The compiler outputs GLSL for WebGL backends or WGSL for WebGPU backends automatically.

WebGPU Shading Language — the shader language for the WebGPU API. Similar in purpose to GLSL but with a Rust-like syntax. Three.js's TSL can compile to WGSL when the WebGPU renderer is used instead of WebGL.

A newer browser GPU API designed to expose more modern GPU capabilities than WebGL, including compute shaders. Supported in recent Chrome and Safari. Three.js added an optional WebGPU renderer alongside its existing WebGL renderer.

A gradient noise algorithm invented by Ken Perlin in the early 1980s that produces smooth, organic-looking randomness without blocky artifacts. Widely used in shaders to simulate natural phenomena — water ripples, terrain, fire, shimmer — by feeding a time-varying noise value into vertex displacement or UV distortion.

A faster, lower-artifact successor to Perlin noise, also developed by Ken Perlin (2001). Uses triangular grid cells instead of square ones, reducing directional artifacts and computational cost — making it preferable for higher-dimensional shader applications.

A physical optical phenomenon where the reflectivity of a surface increases sharply at oblique viewing angles. In game shaders, this is exploited to create rim lighting by brightening the silhouette edges of 3D objects — the computation is a dot product between the surface normal and the camera view direction, making it extremely cheap.

A rendering technique that adds a bright halo to the silhouette edges of a 3D object, visually separating it from the background. In real-time graphics it is typically implemented via a Fresnel shader. Common in sci-fi games, character renders, and force-field effects.

A rendering stage where visual effects are applied to the already-finished 2D image of a 3D scene rather than to the geometry itself. Equivalent to color grading or film-grain added in editing after photography. In Three.js, managed by the EffectComposer pipeline.

A Three.js utility that manages a sequential chain of post-processing shader passes. A RenderPass first captures the 3D scene to a texture, then additional ShaderPasses — bloom, color grade, VHS distortion, etc. — process that texture in order before the final frame is displayed.

A post-processing effect that mimics the visual artifacts of analog video tape: horizontal line displacement, vertical roll, and grain noise. In Three.js it is typically implemented as a ShaderPass using procedural noise. Pieter Levels used a variant in Drones of War to simulate FPV signal degradation with distance.

A technique in which the vertex shader moves mesh vertices away from their rest positions — typically driven by noise or trigonometric wave functions — to simulate organic animation such as tree sway, flag flutter, or water surface movement without requiring additional geometry.

A piloting mode in which live video from a camera mounted on a drone or vehicle is streamed to the operator, simulating the sensation of being inside the craft. In gaming, FPV camera placement creates the same effect. Analog FPV systems are known for their characteristic signal-noise artifacts, which the VHS shader mimics.

A development practice in which AI assistants write the majority of code while the human provides creative direction and high-level intent. The term gained broad use in 2025; the Cursor Vibe Jam formalized it as a competitive rule, requiring that at least 90% of each entry's code be AI-generated.

repos.summary: The core Three.js library — an MIT-licensed JavaScript toolkit for GPU-accelerated 3D graphics in the browser. Created by Ricardo Cabello in 2010, it wraps WebGL (and now WebGPU) in a developer-friendly API. With 112,000+ GitHub stars it is the de-facto standard for browser-based 3D, from data visualizations to games. Version r184 introduced TSL, a node-graph shader API that compiles to GLSL or WGSL.

A Three.js post-processing shader by Felix Turner that simulates VHS and analog TV distortion — horizontal scanline displacement, vertical roll, and procedural grain. Runs as an EffectComposer ShaderPass and uses procedural noise functions to generate its artifacts. This is the shader type Pieter Levels used in Drones of War to simulate FPV video signal loss.

Danny Limanseta's Tiny Skies vibejam entry — a cosy browser flying game where players deliver packages across a small procedural world. Built with Vite, TypeScript, and Three.js on the client and Node.js, Socket.io, and Prisma on the server. The repo accumulated 192 stars after the 2025 jam, notable traction for a game-jam project.
